title: Consolation and desolation
hook: what draws you toward God and what drags you away

segments.voice: Yesterday, the examen: Ignatius's five steps, beginning with thanks. Today, the two words Ignatius used for what you find when you look. And the week ends.

Two evenings. On one, the drive home is light: a kind word given or received, and the world seems roomy. On the other, everything's gray, people get snapped at, and praying, or trying at all, looks pointless. It's easy to file these under good days and bad days. Ignatius wouldn't. In his Spiritual Exercises they're more than moods. They're movements, inner pulls with a direction, and he gives them names. Today's word is the first of the two.
screen: `ONE EVENING, LIGHT.` → `ANOTHER, EVERYTHING'S GRAY.` → `NOT MOODS: MOVEMENTS.`

segments.voice: First, consolation, from the Latin for comfort, being comforted. In his Spiritual Exercises, Ignatius describes it as any inner movement that draws the soul toward God: an increase of faith, hope and love, a deep peace, joy that lifts you toward what matters. Second, desolation, the opposite pull: darkness, restlessness, a drift toward low things, feeling lazy, lukewarm, sad, as if cut off from God. Here's the surprise: consolation isn't the same as feeling good. Tears of sorrow for something you've done wrong can be consolation, because they turn you toward God. And a fun, busy week can hide desolation, if it's quietly pulling you away. The question isn't how do I feel. It's which way am I being pulled. Third, the rules. Ignatius gives advice for both, and one rule is blunt: in desolation, never make a change. Don't quit, don't break up, don't move across the country when everything feels dark. Stay with the decisions you made in a better light, pray a little more, and wait; Ignatius expects it to pass. In consolation, enjoy it, give thanks, and store up strength for the harder days. Fourth, what it means. In Ignatius's reading, desolation isn't proof God has left. He says God can allow it, to teach that consolation is a gift, not something anyone manufactures. This week in camp five: contemplation, the four rungs of lectio divina, read, meditate, pray, rest, then the examen, and now consolation. Every one is a way of paying attention.
screen: `CONSOLATION: DRAWN TOWARD GOD.` · `DESOLATION: DRAGGED AWAY.` · `IN DESOLATION, MAKE NO CHANGE.` · `A GIFT, NOT MANUFACTURED.` · then, large: `WHICH WAY AM I BEING PULLED?`

segments.voice: The examen asked where God was; this asks about direction, so go back over the last day and find the moment you felt most drawn toward life, toward love, toward God if you believe: that's your consolation. Then find the moment you felt most pulled away, dragged down, closed in, and name it without judging: that's your desolation. Notice the direction of each, not just the feeling, and if you pray, bring both to God, the high with thanks, the low with honesty.
Consolation. In Ignatius's language, any movement that draws you toward God, even through tears. Its opposite is desolation. Today's word.
Your line: notice the pull. A heavy mood is no time for a big decision. That's the week.

howItsDone: Catholics who make Ignatian retreats or meet with a spiritual director often talk through their consolations and desolations, using Ignatius's rules for the discernment of spirits to make decisions.
